Discharge of Wastewater Treatment and Controls The Discharger owns and operates a wastewater collection, treatment, and disposal system (Facility) that provides sewerage service to the City of Holtville, which has a population of approximately 6,600. The wastewater treatment plant has a treatment (design) capacity of 0.85 MGD and is located in the SW ¼ of Section 21, T15S, R15E, SBB&M17. Raw sewage first enters the septage receiving station where it’s mixed with air in the septage holding tanks. The raw sewage is then received at the headworks, where it’s passed through a grit chamber to separate solid particles. Wastewater is then mixed with activated sludge in the mixed liquor structure, and it is subsequently directed to a 170 feet (ft) x 124 ft Biolac® aeration basin where air is once again introduced into the sewage water. Wastewater discharged from the Biolac® aeration basin is then passed through two (2) secondary clarifiers (40 ft x 43 ft) in parallel. Sludge collected from the secondary clarifiers is dewatered at a rotary drum thickener and then pumped to six (6) sludge drying beds (three (3) sludge beds measuring 70 ft x 38 ft and three (3) more measuring 92 ft x 40 ft). The sludge drying beds are equipped with sand filters and perforated underdrains. Leachate collected from the drying beds is pumped back to the headworks for reprocessing. The tank is fed from the 6th, treated water is harvested from the 10th, and the settled sludge flows out from the first layer. A fraction of the sludge flows out of the system in the form of waste at a flow rate of 385 m 3 /d, corresponding to a biomass age of 9 days, while the other fraction is recycled externally to the first tank at a rate of 18,446 m 3 /d. The biological processes occurring in both biological reactors are simulated using the IWA Activated Sludge Model No. 1 (ASM1) proposed by [47] . This model uses thirteen state variables to track the fate of biodegradable, non-biodegradable, soluble, insoluble, nitrogen, and carbon materials. These state variables are linked to eight degradation bioprocesses occurring in biological reactors.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . chunks.text: With the rapid development of industrialization and modernization, the global production of wastewater has grown significantly. As a byproduct of wastewater treatment, the production of sludge has increased substantially accordingly, leading to a dramatic increase in energy consumption (E c ) and disposal costs. Municipal sludge poses a series of challenges for further disposal because of high moisture content (M c ). Therefore, sludge dewatering is the primary step for achieving sludge reduction, harmless treatment, and resource recovery [5, 41] . Mechanical press filtration (MPF) is one of the most commonly used for sludge dewatering. This method can reduce M c of sludge to 60-80 %, which cannot meet the current and future lower M c requirements [30] . MPF can only remove the relatively easy-to-remove free water and causes clogging and deformation of the micro-pore and voids in sludge cake [31] . Therefore, to address this issue, equipment optimization and pressure parameters optimization have been the significant research topics, such as using ultra-high MPF. Iritani et al. [16] studied dewatering under ultrasonic pretreatment at 50 MPa, reducing M c of sludge to 38 %.

chunks.text: The drying facility is located in a large Polish wastewater treatment plant and is composed of 4 lines. The scheme of one drying line is presented in Fig. 1 . Dewatered sludge is collected in a silo from where it is dosed to drum dryers. The temperature in the drum dryers is maintained at ca. 240-260 • C using hot oil. Sludge is uniformly distributed in the drum with paddles. The sludge retention time in the drier is 1-2 min, and the sludge layer in the drum is 1-2 cm thick. Water from the sludge is evaporated and flows as condensate with process air through a purification system composed of a Venturi orifice and two scrubbers, where it is then rinsed with the process water (secondary effluent from the wastewater treatment plant). The biological compartment is made up of two or three tanks (depending on the plant configuration adopted), each with a volume of 7.5 m 3 . After the biological compartment, a secondary settler removes solids before discharge. chunks.text: In the activated sludge process the majority of biological solids removed in the secondary sedimentation tank are recycled (returned sludge). The feedback of most of the cell yields from the sedimentation tank encourages rapid adsorption of the pollutants in the incoming settled sewage and also serves to stabilize the operation over a wide range of dilution rates and substrate concentrations imposed by fluctuations in the flow and strength of the wastewater. Secondary treatment processes can remove up to 95 per cent of the BOD and suspended solids entering the process, as well as significant amounts of heavy metals and certain organic compounds which could otherwise cause the deterioration of chemical and ecological quality of receiving waters [10, 53] . Conventional wastewater treatment usually ends with secondary treatment which cannot efficiently remove all the different compounds found in sewage and therefore treated effluents are one of the main sources of persistent micropollutants in the environment [1, 62] . For water reuse, tertiary treatment is needed to provide additional removal of contaminants such as microbial pathogens, particulates, or nutrients, and advanced treatment processes are employed when wastewater is to be reclaimed for reuse, depending on the type of use and quality requirements [49] .

chunks.text: Based on a survey on pre-treatment measures for 17 full-scale AeMBRs, the following information deserves special attention (Itokawa et al., 2008) : 1) grit chamber, coarse and fine screenings are mostly essential for MBR operation to removal grits, large suspended particles and long fibers, with fine screening (3 mm for FS membrane and 0.5-1 mm for HF membrane) installed universally; and 2) using the "by pass sieving" method, which recycles part of the suspended sludge through a sieve, achieves the further removal of unfavorable substances accumulated in the bioreactor. These means can be extended to AnMBRs minimizing the presence of undesirable substances into the bioreactor while with adequate consideration of keeping strict anaerobic environment. A recent novel concept, referred to as wastewater pre-concentration (Ansari et al., 2016) , is still under investigation, but has shown great potential to enhance bioresource recovery and energy generation efficiency (Guven et al., 2019) , accompanied by a low volumetric flow rate and process footprint (Alvarado et al., 2020) .
